slides.title: What HTTPS gives you
slides.summary: TLS encrypts traffic, proves the server's identity and detects tampering.
body: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS. It gives three guarantees between the browser and the server:

ul: Confidentiality: nobody on the network (café Wi-Fi, ISP) can read the traffic.
Integrity: nobody can change it in flight, e.g. to inject ads or scripts.
Authentication: the certificate proves you're talking to the real domain.

body: <mark>Service workers, geolocation, camera, clipboard and most modern APIs only work on secure origins.</mark>

body.note: TLS 1.3 sets up a new connection in one round trip, and HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which builds TLS 1.3 into the transport.

steps.caption: The server proves who it is.

item.label: Verify
item.sub: Chains to a trusted CA, name matches, not expired

steps.caption: From here on, all traffic is encrypted.

slides.title: Getting HTTPS right
slides.summary: Redirect to HTTPS, add HSTS, avoid mixed content, keep cookies Secure and automate certificates.

ul: HSTS tells browsers never to try HTTP again. Submit the domain to the preload list to protect the very first visit.
No mixed content: an HTTPS page loading http:// resources undoes the protection. Browsers upgrade or block it.
Secure cookies: mark them Secure so they're never sent over HTTP.
Automate certificates with ACME (e.g. Let's Encrypt) or your CDN.

body: <mark>Without HSTS, the first plain-HTTP request can be intercepted and the user kept on a fake HTTP copy of your site.</mark>

body.text: The CA/Browser Forum voted in 2025 to cut maximum certificate lifetimes: 200 days from March 2026, 100 days from March 2027, and 47 days from March 2029. Manual renewal stops being practical, so automate it now.

viz.html: upgrade-insecure-requests in your CSP rewrites leftover http:// subresource URLs to https://.

figure.alt: Two rows. Without HSTS: the user types bank.example, the browser sends http://bank.example over café Wi-Fi, an attacker on the network intercepts it and keeps the user on a plain-HTTP copy of the site (SSL stripping), reading passwords and cookies. With HSTS: the browser remembers, or has preloaded, that bank.example is HTTPS-only, upgrades the request internally before anything is sent, and connects with TLS; the attacker sees only encrypted traffic, and certificate errors cannot be clicked through.
